Only the fraud-detection use case genuinely needed sub-second latency, so the team added a focused streaming path (Kafka plus a stream processor) just for that, while converting the relevant dashboards to micro-batch and leaving the rest of the platform on batch. Leadership got the responsiveness they actually wanted, and the team avoided rebuilding everything as streaming and the enormous operational burden that would have entailed.

nestedTopics.title: Clarifying what 'real-time' really means
nestedTopics.explanation: 'Real-time' is ambiguous, ranging from sub-second to 'within a few minutes,' and the genuine requirement drastically changes the right solution and its cost. The essential first step is pinning down the actual freshness need per use case and the business value of that latency, because many requests labeled 'real-time' are satisfied by data that's minutes fresh, which is far cheaper to deliver than true streaming. Challenging the vague ask with concrete questions is what prevents over-building.

nestedTopics.title: Micro-batch as the pragmatic middle
nestedTopics.explanation: Micro-batch, processing small batches every few seconds or minutes, delivers near-real-time latency while keeping much of batch's simplicity and reusable logic, and avoiding the full operational weight of true event streaming. For a large share of 'real-time-ish' needs like dashboards refreshing every minute, it's the pragmatic sweet spot. Reaching for micro-batch before true streaming often satisfies the requirement at a fraction of the complexity and cost.

nestedTopics.title: Incremental introduction of streaming
nestedTopics.explanation: For needs that genuinely require true low latency, the right approach is to add a streaming path incrementally for those specific use cases, alongside the existing batch platform, rather than rebuilding everything as streaming. This contains the new complexity to where it's justified, lets the proven batch platform keep serving everything else, and reduces risk. Evolving the platform additively beats a risky, expensive big-bang re-architecture.

nestedTopics.title: Total cost of ownership of streaming
nestedTopics.explanation: True streaming carries ongoing costs beyond building it: 24/7 operation, always-on resources, on-call coverage, harder debugging, state and checkpoint management, and new skills the team may need to acquire. These must be weighed against the business value of low latency before committing, because the operational burden is substantial and recurring. Recognizing this full cost, not just the build effort, is what separates a sound decision from chasing a buzzword.

followUps.question: What questions do you ask leadership before building real-time infrastructure?
followUps.answer: I focus on uncovering the genuine requirement and its value, because 'real-time' is often a vague aspiration that, examined closely, turns out to mean something much cheaper to deliver. Key questions: which specific use cases need to be real-time, and what would users actually do differently with second-fresh data versus minute-fresh or hour-fresh data, this reveals whether the latency creates real value or just sounds good. How fresh, exactly, does each case need to be (sub-second, seconds, minutes), since that determines whether micro-batch suffices or true streaming is required. What's the business cost of the current batch latency, and what's the expected return from reducing it, so the investment can be justified. Is this for monitoring/alerting (inherently event-driven, may need streaming) or just fresher reporting (often micro-batch). And practically, does the team have or can it acquire the capacity to operate streaming 24/7. These questions let me separate the use cases that genuinely warrant streaming's cost and complexity from the larger set satisfied by faster batch, so I can propose a solution scoped to real needs rather than building expensive infrastructure for latency nobody actually benefits from, which is the central judgment the scenario is testing.

followUps.question: Why not just rebuild the whole platform as streaming?
followUps.answer: Because it would take on enormous cost, risk, and complexity to serve needs most of the platform doesn't have. The vast majority of analytical workloads, daily and historical reporting, don't benefit from real-time at all, so converting them to streaming adds the heavy operational burden of 24/7 operation, always-on resources, on-call, state management, and harder debugging with zero business upside for that data. A full rebuild is also extremely risky: re-architecting a working, trusted batch platform wholesale invites instability and data issues during the transition, jeopardizing things that currently work fine. And it's wasteful, streaming is more expensive to run, so paying that for data that's only ever consumed daily is pure cost. The pragmatic alternative is to introduce streaming incrementally and only where genuine low-latency needs exist, keeping the proven batch platform for everything else, which contains the new complexity to where it's justified, preserves stability, and matches spend to value. Rebuilding everything as streaming is the classic over-engineering trap, chasing architectural uniformity or buzzword appeal rather than serving actual requirements, and the senior move is to evolve additively and scope streaming to real needs, not to impose it universally.

followUps.question: How do you minimize maintaining two separate codebases for batch and streaming?
followUps.answer: This is a real concern, since running both batch and streaming risks the dual-codebase problem, duplicated logic that drifts and doubles maintenance, the same pain that pushed the industry from Lambda toward Kappa. I minimize it with a few strategies. First, I use engines and frameworks that unify batch and streaming, Spark Structured Streaming and Flink let you express transformations once and run them in either mode, and table formats like Delta, Iceberg, and Hudi support both batch and streaming reads/writes to the same tables, so much logic can be shared rather than reimplemented. Second, I factor the actual business logic into reusable components that both paths invoke, so the transformation rules live in one place even if the execution mode differs. Third, where true streaming is only needed for a few specific use cases, I keep that footprint small so there's minimal duplicated surface to maintain, rather than mirroring the entire batch platform. The goal is to share definitions and logic across the two modes as much as the tooling allows, treating batch and streaming as different runtimes over common logic rather than wholly separate implementations, so I get the low latency where needed without paying the maintenance tax of two diverging codebases, which is exactly the lesson behind preferring unified, incremental approaches over parallel Lambda-style duplication.
